title: The Mystery of the Beep-less Alarm
markdown:
The sky rumbled first. Then came the quiet where a beep should have been.

Dex’s workshop whirred and tap-tapped. He tested inventions for POP or fizzle, and kept a towel on a hook because fizzle was more common than anyone admitted. Biscuit, a scruffy terrier mix, conducted a tail-symphony for every gadget and sometimes conducted the toolbox onto the floor. A screw rolled under the bench. Biscuit considered it a prize.

Dr. Hale had made a Rainy Day Alarm: a sensor like a clever nose for the sky, meant to beep a cheerful warning before boots were needed. Her glasses sat a little crooked and twinkled when she was pleased. “No more getting caught.” She left it on the windowsill as if the sill were a proper weather station.

One afternoon the sky went bruised-plum. Grey giants of cloud marched the sun down. Dex had already put a hand on the door. The alarm’s red light glowed. No beep. No peep. Biscuit nudged his hand, questioning wag. Then the sky opened. Rain drowned the windows and gurgled in the gutter. They were soaked before they could blink. Water ran off Dex’s fringe in a tidy, insulting line.

He shook a bird’s-nest of wet hair. “What’s wrong with its rainy-day sense?” The sensor was a smooth grey disc, heavy, beaded with droplets. “It’s wet,” he told Biscuit, who shook and shared the weather with the nearest notebook.

Dr. Hale arrived with a fluffy towel and a smile that did not scold. “Sensors measure one thing. We have to know which thing, not which thing we hoped for.” She wiped the disc until the beads became a smear and then nothing. “This doesn’t count raindrops. It measures air pressure.”

“The air being squeezed?”

“Before rain, pressure often drops — a sigh from the sky. The sensor felt a drop. But pressure drops for other reasons too: a gust, a big bird, even a herd of grumble-goblins, which we have not hosted lately. The drop it felt was not the kind that definitely meant a soaking.”

Dex looked from disc to dripping glass. The red light had been honest about a change and silent about boots. “If it measures pressure, and a big drop can mean rain… what if we made that kind of drop more obvious?” Biscuit’s tail hoped on the floorboards.

They rummaged. Dex found a tiny super-light fan, the desk-cooler sort, and fixed it so it could spin free above the disc. “A real drop should push this. Hard enough, it spins. A little weather-vane.” Hale held the screwdriver still while he tightened the last screw. Biscuit supervised from the stool and did not eat the washer.

They waited. The workshop held its breath. Sky went brooding grey. A gentle breeze left the fan still. A stronger gust rattled the panes. The fan hummed, then whirled. At its fastest, fat drops splat the glass, then a steady drumming. Dex counted three spins before the first splat, then stopped counting because he was grinning.

“It worked.” Biscuit agreed in bark.

Hale’s spectacles glinted. She did not lecture about detectives and planets. “It reports what it actually feels. You gave the report a way to be seen.”

Dex picked up the modified alarm. The fan ticked once more and settled. “Not just a rainy-day box. A pressure-change box that happens to help with rain.” He wrote PRESSURE first on a scrap, then RAIN in smaller letters underneath, so the job and the hope would not get swapped again. Biscuit licked his chin, punctuation. They hung a towel by the door and watched the fan spin down as the drumming eased. The next cloud, when it came, would have to mean it.
